title: Free up storage space on Mac
fact_scope: Apple defines System Data as a broad category for Apple and third-party files that do not fit another category. Moving an item to Trash does not make its storage available until Trash is emptied. Safe mode may clear some caches that macOS recreates.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. Use for system behavior, not user prevalence or deletion authorization.

title: Find and delete files on your Mac
fact_scope: macOS Storage categories vary with installed apps and files. System Data includes logs, caches, VM files, runtime resources, temporary files, fonts, app support, and plug-ins. The guide separates free space from available space and notes that Finder or the creating app may manage user data.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. The category description is not a complete inventory of removable items.

title: Delete files and folders on Mac
fact_scope: macOS moves deleted items to Trash before they are deleted. Finder can put a trashed item back, and locked items may require an additional confirmation.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. Trash recovery does not prove that the content is otherwise disposable.

title: About Time Machine local snapshots
fact_scope: Time Machine can keep local snapshots on the startup disk when the backup disk is unavailable. macOS removes them as they age or when space is needed, and Apple describes a separate manual settings path for temporary removal.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. Do not assume a snapshot is stale or safe to remove from size alone.

title: About Time Machine local snapshots on Mac
fact_scope: Local snapshots are separate from the external backup disk, can remain for up to 24 hours or until space is needed, and are only stored on APFS disks when automatic backups are enabled.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. The user guide supports explaining snapshot state, not silently deleting it.

title: View APFS snapshots in Disk Utility on Mac
fact_scope: Disk Utility can list APFS snapshots and expose identifiers, creation dates, private size, cumulative size, and kind. It also presents an explicit delete action for selected snapshots.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. Snapshot metadata should be shown as a distinct state from ordinary files.

title: Change Privacy & Security settings on Mac
fact_scope: macOS separates Files & Folders permission from Full Disk Access. Full Disk Access can expose files from other apps, Time Machine backups, and administrative settings, so the permission scope is material to a storage scan.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. Use the smallest useful scope and explain it before opening the system prompt.

title: Control access to files and folders on Mac
fact_scope: macOS lets users grant or deny third-party access to specific locations such as Desktop, Downloads, and Documents. Apple points users to the app's privacy practices when granting access.
quality_note: First-party platform guidance. Permission requests are part of the product experience and trust decision.

title: File Provider
fact_scope: File Provider manages local copies of remote documents and can expose dataless or materialized items. The framework includes domains, item capabilities, sync controls, and error states.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. File Provider ownership and state must remain distinct from ordinary local files.

title: Synchronizing the File Provider Extension
fact_scope: A File Provider can keep dataless and materialized local copies, convert materialized items to dataless copies to save disk space, and protect items with pending changes from that conversion. Its working set includes recently used, tagged, shared, and recently deleted items.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. A visible path and a local byte count do not fully describe remote ownership or sync state.

title: NSFileProviderDomain
fact_scope: File Provider domains partition content and can represent different accounts or locations. The API exposes user-enabled, disconnected, replicated-known-folder, and syncing-trash state.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. Tessera should name the domain or owner when it can, and hand off actions it cannot verify.

title: NSFileProviderManager
fact_scope: The manager API can enumerate domains, translate user-visible URLs, track global upload or download progress, wait for stabilization, disconnect or reconnect domains, and request diagnostics.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. Owner-aware actions need state and stabilization checks, not path matching alone.

title: supportsSyncingTrash
fact_scope: A File Provider domain exposes whether it supports syncing Trash, which can change the meaning of a move-to-Trash action for remote-backed content.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. A Trash action must not be described as local-only when the owner can sync it.

title: FileManager trashItem(at:resultingItemURL:)
fact_scope: Foundation exposes a trash operation that moves an item to Trash and can return the resulting URL because the item name or location may change during the move.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. Record the resulting Trash URL and per-item outcome instead of assuming the original path remains valid.

title: NSFileCoordinator
fact_scope: NSFileCoordinator coordinates reads, writes, moves, and deletes among file presenters and other processes. It can notify interested owners before a change and may pass a changed URL to the operation.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. Coordination is a safety tool, not proof that an owner process has no other live state.

title: NSFileCoordinator.WritingOptions
fact_scope: The file coordination API has explicit writing options for deleting and moving. Coordinated access can wait for file presenters and can fail before the write block runs.
quality_note: First-party API documentation. Use the delete or move intent explicitly and surface coordination failures to the user.
